projects.tagline: Ant colony optimisation for mobile ad hoc networks: the colony the org grew out of.
summary: AntHocNet (Di Caro, Ducatelle & Gambardella, 2005) routes like a foraging colony. When a data packet finds no route, the source sends **reactive forward ants** that search towards the destination; each one flips into a **backward ant** there and walks the path home, laying pheromone that scores each next hop. The backward ant is the only thing that deposits regular pheromone.

While a session runs, **proactive ants** keep sampling and improving the path, **hello** beacons keep the neighbour set fresh and diffuse a virtual pheromone, and when a link breaks the node sends **repair** ants or a **LinkFail** notification upstream. Data follows the pheromone stochastically, so load spreads over several good paths.

The algorithm is written once, as a simulator-agnostic `core/` (C++14) that takes time, randomness, neighbours and timers through ports. The ns-3 module and the browser adapter only convert headers and carry out the core's `RouteDecision`s; the game here runs that same `core/` compiled to WebAssembly, byte-identical to the native trace.

projects.tagline: The Ant-Colony-Based Routing Algorithm: reactive ants, data that reinforces its own path.
summary: ARA (Güneş, Sorges & Bouazizi, 2002) is the lean ancestor in the family. Route discovery floods a **forward ant (FANT)** from the source; every node it reaches records pheromone back towards the source. The destination answers with a **backward ant (BANT)**, which sets up pheromone towards the destination on the way back.

After discovery there are no maintenance ants: **data packets themselves reinforce** the pheromone of the links they use, and pheromone **evaporates** over time, so unused routes fade. Duplicate packets are detected by sequence number to stop loops, and a broken link makes the node try another next hop before reporting a route error upstream.

Here ARA becomes a standalone protocol on the org's hexagonal pattern: a fresh simulator-agnostic `core/` on `swarm-core`, the ns-3 module `ara`, a fidelity sheet citing the paper for every parameter, then the three comparator gates. It replaces AntHocNet's `ara` comparator arm.

projects.tagline: Honeybee foraging as routing: scouts find paths, foragers carry data, the dance floor recruits.
summary: BeeAdHoc (Wedde & Farooq, 2005) maps a hive onto each node. **Packers** hold outgoing data at the node. When no route is known, **scouts** are broadcast towards the destination and come back to the source's **dance floor** with the path they found. **Foragers** then carry data along those source routes and return with what they measured, such as delay and residual battery.

On the dance floor a forager's *dance* recruits others in proportion to the quality of its route, so good paths attract more traffic without any global table. The energy metric reads residual battery through swarm-core's `EnergyMetricHook` over `ns3::EnergySource`.

Where the sources disagree (GECCO 2005, the PG 439 / PG 460 reports, Farooq's thesis), each interpretation is pre-registered in an issue, with its evidence, before code. AntHocNet's BeeAdHoc arm missed its PG 460 anchor on 3 of 5 pause times, so those fidelity questions come first.

projects.tagline: Routing by stigmergy: the pheromone rides inside the data packets themselves.
summary: Termite (Roth & Wicker; GLOBECOM 2003, SIDM 2005, Roth's 2005 dissertation) has **no control ants**. Every data packet carries routing state: as a packet arrives, the receiving node strengthens its pheromone towards the packet's **source** through the neighbour it came from. Traffic in one direction builds the routes for traffic in the other.

Forwarding is **randomised multipath**: the next hop is drawn in proportion to pheromone, and pheromone **decays** with time, so the table tracks a moving topology without beacons of its own. What a node does with a packet for a destination it holds no pheromone for is one of the questions the fidelity sheet settles from the dissertation.

AntHocNet's Termite arm passed the delivery smoke but missed its anchor in v2.5.0 (trend right, confidence intervals spanning zero). Whether that was the arm, the scenario or statistical power is pre-registered in an issue before `core/` is written.

projects.tagline: Ants that hop between routing zones: proactive inside a zone, reactive between zones.
summary: HOPNET (Wang, 2007 MSc thesis, University of Manitoba) crosses ant colony routing with **zone routing**. Each node keeps a zone of nodes within a few hops. Inside the zone, routes are kept **proactively**; towards a destination outside it, **forward ants hop from zone border to zone border** instead of flooding every node, and backward ants bring the path home.

It is the one published result found that benchmarks against AntHocNet directly, claiming better scaling, so its anchor pairs the two through ns3-tools with the AntHocNet configuration pinned and stated. No AntHocNet code exists for it: `core/` is written fresh from the thesis.

projects.tagline: What two or more protocols share: the swarm-core contrib module every protocol links against.
summary: `swarm-core` is the shared ns-3 contrib module (`libns3.<ver>-swarm-core`, `#include "ns3/swarm-core-module.h"`). Its `core/` will hold simulator-free C++20 primitives extracted from AntHocNet's dual-licensed core: the bounded `VisitedPath`, little-endian wire helpers, `PheromoneTable`, `RouteDecision`, the `ILinkState` / `ILinkMetric` seams, evaporation and roulette selection.

Its `model/` will hold the ns-3 glue: `SwarmRoutingBase`, a `DeferredPacketQueue`, `WifiLinkMonitor`, `EnergyMetricHook` over `ns3::EnergySource`, and `IslLinkMonitor` for satellite links. Nothing protocol-specific lands here: code is promoted only when a second protocol needs it.

Today the skeleton is in place (`kSwarmCoreApiVersion`, `SwarmCoreSeed`) and CI already runs every org quality gate on it: strict warnings, debug and sanitized builds, coverage, format, licence headers, and the determinism gate (same seed twice byte-identical, another seed different).

projects.tagline: Protocol-agnostic comparison: the harness every arm registers with, and the scripts that judge the runs.
summary: ns3-tools is where protocols meet on equal terms. The `routing-bench` module (moved from AntHocNet as-is) is the comparison harness: every protocol, ours or a comparator, registers as an **arm** through its own `helper/<module>-bench-arms.cc`, and no arm is special-cased. It also holds the measurement itself today: the topology oracle (BFS-reachable delivery ratio, path stretch) and the drop book (PHY/MAC/ARP/TTL/loop root causes). A run prints the versioned marker lines `##CONFIG##`, `##RUN##`, `##BENCH##`, `##DIAG##` and `##PROV##`.

The `ns3-tool` CLI (`compare`, `sweep`, `diagnose`, `scaffold`) fronts the Python readers (stdlib only): they parse those lines and do the statistics, per-seed paired deltas over at least 20 seeds and a scripted noise verdict, never an eyeballed one, checked byte-identical against fixture cells from AntHocNet. `ns3-campaign` runs a multi-protocol campaign: one image, every cell pulled by digest, each keyed over every pinned input. The CLI and marker contract v1 are frozen: fields, commands and options are only appended, and a breaking change waits for contract v2.

Planned next: non-intrusive probes as their own module (the oracle and the drop book extracted), the satellite harnesses on the arm registry, and the non-swarm comparator arms, each its own module under `ns3/arms/`. Whether the universal arenas of the original plan stay is an open decision.

projects.tagline: ns-3 pre-built and tested, so a contrib module compiles alone in seconds.
summary: ns3-containers publishes `ghcr.io/swarm-routing/ns3-dev` (public, no login): ns-3 configured and built with Ninja at `/opt/ns-3`. A downstream module is linked into the warm tree by `ns3-build-contrib` and compiles alone; the smoke gate counts the Ninja steps (8 today, gate 40) to prove the cache was hit.

Automatic pipelines build only the release ns-3 supports (its latest), read from upstream's tags by `tools/ns3_matrix.py`, never a hand-typed version. Older releases are built on demand and kept as history. Four profiles: `default`, `debug` (CI), `sanitized` (ASan + LSan + UBSan) and `optimized` (ns-3's `release`, for campaigns only, never `-march=native`).

**What is tested is what is tagged:** each image is built once, every test stage runs on that build by digest (structure, profile, smoke, integration, unit, Trivy security), and the published tags are a carbon copy of that digest, then signed and attested. A published number pins the immutable `:<ver>-<profile>-<sha7>` tag.

The image pipeline itself is versioned: a release archives the Dockerfile, `ns3-build-contrib`, the test stages and `tools/` at a commit, while an image tag stays the ns-3 release it was built from. Before a `latest-*` tag moves, the downstream canary builds and tests every org module on the new image.

projects.tagline: Immutable, reproducible benchmark datasets: every number traceable to its image, commits and seeds.
summary: benchmarks will hold the org's evidence: 20-seed `##RUN##` / `##BENCH##` data, the paired statistical verdicts recomputed from it, and a **manifest** for every run pinning the immutable `ns3-dev:<ver>-<profile>-<sha7>` image, each protocol's commit, the scenario, the seeds and the exact command line. No manifest, no merge.

Merged data is **immutable**: a correction is a new run that names the one it supersedes. Campaigns run on the `optimized` image; CI legs use `debug` and `sanitized`. The Colony Arena's leaderboard (site#12) will be regenerated from these verdicts by a script, never typed by hand.
